```{python}
#| tags: [setup]
import sys, os
sys.path.insert(0, os.path.abspath("."))
from _pcpkg import *  # noqa: F401,F403
import doe_report as D
import tables as T          # complex tables: merged cells, footnotes (T.<builder>(...).show())
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import scipy.stats as sstat

DOC = "PCR-008"
UO = "aex"
UO_TITLE = "Anion Exchange Chromatography (Step 8)"

import itertools
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
from amab_process import iac as _iac, load_config as _load_config

# --- the step, its parameters and how a value is written ---------------------------------
UOP = CFG.unit_op(UO)
P = {p.key: p for p in UOP.parameters}
FS = D.rsm_factors(UO)                                   # the four parameters of the designs
UNI = [k for k in P if P[k].study == "univariate"]
assert UNI == ["flow"] and len(FS) == 4
LET = D.factor_letters(UO)
RESP = D.responses(UO)                                   # hcp, xmulv, mvm, step yield
FRAG = "lmw_cesds_pct"
CRIT_OUT = [r for r in RESP + [FRAG] if D.effective_acceptance(UO, r) is not None]
assert CRIT_OUT == ["hcp_out_ng_mg", "xmulv_lrf", "mvm_lrf", FRAG]
TH = THRESHOLDS
ALPHA = float(TH["effect_alpha"])
GAPMAX = float(TH["max_r2_minus_pred_r2"])


def mn(x):
    """A true minus sign."""
    return str(x).replace("-", "−")


def fx(x, nd=2):
    return mn(f"{float(x):,.{nd}f}")


def fp(p):
    return "< 0.001" if p < 0.001 else f"{p:.3f}"


def pn(k):
    """A parameter name inside a sentence (from the config)."""
    n = P[k].name
    w = n.split()[0]
    return n if ("/" in w or w.isupper()) else n[0].lower() + n[1:]


def PN(k):
    return P[k].name


def qv(k, v, nd=None):
    """A value of parameter k with its unit (a pH carries none)."""
    s = f"{float(v):g}" if nd is None else f"{float(v):.{nd}f}"
    u = P[k].unit
    return s if u == "pH" else f"{s} {u}"


def qr(k, lo, hi, nd=None):
    f_ = (lambda v: f"{float(v):g}") if nd is None else (lambda v: f"{float(v):.{nd}f}")
    u = P[k].unit
    return f"{f_(lo)}–{f_(hi)}" + ("" if u == "pH" else f" {u}")


NORS = {k: qr(k, *P[k].nor) for k in P}
RNGS = {k: qr(k, *P[k].prange) for k in P}
SPS = {k: qv(k, P[k].setpoint) for k in P}
# no NOR or set-point of this step was changed at Version 2.0
NO_NOR_CHANGE = all(tuple(map(float, P[k].nor)) == tuple(map(float, P[k].nor_characterized))
                    and float(P[k].setpoint) == float(P[k].setpoint_characterized) for k in P)
assert NO_NOR_CHANGE
# the middle of each characterized range (coded 0) and the set-point
MID = {k: (P[k].prange[0] + P[k].prange[1]) / 2 for k in FS}
MID_NE_SP = [k for k in FS if abs(MID[k] - P[k].setpoint) > 1e-9]
assert MID_NE_SP == ["load"]

# --- studies, dates, records -----------------------------------------------------------
CHRON = csv("study_chronology.csv")
CHRON = CHRON[CHRON["step"] == UO].set_index("id")
W = {i: (r["start"], r["end"]) for i, r in CHRON.iterrows()}
MA = CFG.raw()["campaign"]["model_adequacy"]
AUG_ID = MA["studies"][UO]["id"]
assert AUG_ID in W
SCR = csv("doe_aex_screening.csv")
RSM = csv("doe_aex_rsm.csv")
AUGD = csv("doe_aex_aug.csv")
n_scr, n_rsm, n_aug = doe_runs(UO, "screening"), doe_runs(UO, "rsm"), len(AUGD)
n_all = n_rsm + n_aug
n_cp_scr, n_cp_rsm = doe_centre_points(UO, "screening"), doe_centre_points(UO, "rsm")
n_fact = int((RSM["run_type"] == "factorial").sum())
n_axial = int((RSM["run_type"] == "axial").sum())
assert int((SCR["run_type"] == "factorial").sum()) == 2 ** len(FS) == n_fact
assert n_scr == n_fact + n_cp_scr and n_rsm == n_fact + n_axial + n_cp_rsm
aug_first, aug_last = int(AUGD["run"].min()), int(AUGD["run"].max())
# centre points and axial runs at coded 0 sit at the middle of the range
assert np.allclose(RSM.loc[RSM["run_type"] == "center", "load"], MID["load"])
LOTS = csv("dev_lots.csv").set_index("id")
DEVF = dev_facts(DOC).set_index("dev_id")
n_events = len(DEVF)
PDS = PLAN_DISCREPANCIES[DOC]
n_pd = len(PDS)
PD = {d["subject"]: d["id"] for d in PDS}
PD_AUG = PD["Augmentation of the response-surface design"]
PD_SEL = PD["Model selection for the response-surface outputs"]
PD_FLOW = [d["id"] for d in PDS if d["id"] not in (PD_AUG, PD_SEL)][0]
assert n_events == 3 and n_pd == 3
PRIOR = csv("dev_prior_docs.csv").set_index("id")
METH = csv("dev_methods.csv").set_index("id")
CESDS = CFG.raw()["analytics"]["methods"]["cesds"]

# --- fitted models ----------------------------------------------------------------------
FIT = {r: D.fit(UO, "rsm", r) for r in RESP + [FRAG]}
RI = {r: D.residual_influence(UO, r) for r in RESP + [FRAG]}
assert all(FIT[r]["status"] == "selected" for r in RESP + [FRAG])
assert all(RI[r]["met"] for r in RESP + [FRAG]) and not any(RI[r]["over_f"] for r in RESP + [FRAG])
HCP, XM, MV, YLD = "hcp_out_ng_mg", "xmulv_lrf", "mvm_lrf", "step_yield"
assert FIT[HCP]["transform"] == "log" and all(FIT[r]["transform"] is None for r in (XM, MV, YLD, FRAG))
assert FIT[HCP]["names"] == ["load_ph", "wash1_cond"] and FIT[MV]["names"] == ["load_ph", "load_cond"]
assert FIT[XM]["names"] == ["load_ph", "load_cond", "load", "load_ph:load"]
assert FIT[YLD]["names"] == [] and FIT[FRAG]["names"] == []
assert FIT[HCP]["block"] and FIT[YLD]["block"] and FIT[FRAG]["block"] and not FIT[XM]["block"]
BC = FIT[HCP]["boxcox"]
assert BC["lo"] <= 0 <= BC["hi"] < 1
FP = {r: D.fit(UO, "rsm", r, runs="planned") for r in RESP + [FRAG]}
FF = {r: D.fit(UO, "rsm", r, runs="planned", form="full") for r in RESP + [FRAG]}
assert not any(FF[r]["adequate"] for r in CRIT_OUT)          # the plan's model fails §7.2 for all four
assert FP[YLD]["status"] == "none" and FP[HCP]["names"] == FIT[HCP]["names"]
HCPm = FIT[HCP]["model"]
bA, bB, bBlk = (float(HCPm.params[k]) for k in ("load_ph", "wash1_cond", "block"))
fold_A, fold_B = np.exp(2 * bA), np.exp(2 * bB)
mult_sd = np.exp(FIT[HCP]["rmse"])
# raw-scale residual scatter of the same terms, lower and upper half of the predictions
_d = FIT[HCP]["df"]
_mr = sm.OLS(_d[HCP].to_numpy(float), D.ad.matrix(_d, FIT[HCP]["names"], True).to_numpy(float)).fit()
_med = float(np.median(_mr.fittedvalues))
raw_sd_lo = float(np.std(_mr.resid[_mr.fittedvalues <= _med], ddof=1))
raw_sd_hi = float(np.std(_mr.resid[_mr.fittedvalues > _med], ddof=1))
_ml = HCPm
_medl = float(np.median(_ml.fittedvalues))
log_sd_lo = float(np.std(_ml.resid[_ml.fittedvalues <= _medl], ddof=1))
log_sd_hi = float(np.std(_ml.resid[_ml.fittedvalues > _medl], ddof=1))
assert raw_sd_hi > raw_sd_lo
XMm, MVm = FIT[XM]["model"], FIT[MV]["model"]
xA, xC, xD, xAD = (float(XMm.params[k]) for k in ("load_ph", "load_cond", "load", "load_ph:load"))
mA, mC = (float(MVm.params[k]) for k in ("load_ph", "load_cond"))
# the change of XMuLV LRF from the lowest to the highest protein load, at each end of load pH
xD_lo, xD_hi = 2 * (xD - xAD), 2 * (xD + xAD)
REP_X, REP_M = float(METH.loc["AMV-3017", "precision_pct"]), float(METH.loc["AMV-3018", "precision_pct"])
N_SUBSETS = len(D.ad.hierarchical_subsets(FS))

# selection by exhaustive search against stepwise search (INV-002)
SCMP = D.selection_comparison()
_sc = SCMP[~SCMP["exact"]]
n_sc = len(_sc)
n_bw_worse, n_fw_worse = int(_sc["backward_worse"].sum()), int(_sc["forward_worse"].sum())
SC_AEX = _sc[_sc["step_key"] == UO].set_index("response")
AUGCHK = D.augmentation_prediction_check()
AUGCHK = AUGCHK[AUGCHK["step_key"] == UO].set_index("response")

# --- near-equivalent models and the deletion of flagged runs -----------------------------
_NOR_NAT = list(itertools.product(*[[P[f].nor[0], P[f].setpoint, P[f].nor[1]] for f in FS]))
_NOR_C = pd.DataFrame({f: [float(D.to_coded(UO, f, g[i])) for g in _NOR_NAT] for i, f in enumerate(FS)})
n_nor = len(_NOR_C)
DS_N = 11
_CUBE = pd.DataFrame(list(itertools.product(*[np.linspace(-1, 1, DS_N)] * len(FS))), columns=FS)
OFF = D.sdm_offset(UO, HCP)
QUAL = D.offset_qualification(UO, HCP)
assert OFF["scale"] == "ratio" and QUAL["qualified"] and QUAL["met_lo"] and QUAL["met_hi"]


def _refit(resp, d, terms, block, log):
    y = np.log(d[resp].to_numpy(float)) if log else d[resp].to_numpy(float)
    m = sm.OLS(y, D.ad.matrix(d, terms, block).to_numpy(float)).fit()
    return {"factors": FS, "names": list(terms), "quad": True, "block": bool(block), "model": m, "log": log}


def _pi(r, coded):
    sf = r["model"].get_prediction(D._design_matrix(r, coded)).summary_frame(alpha=1 - D.PI_LEVEL)
    b = np.exp if r["log"] else (lambda v: v)
    return b(sf["mean"].to_numpy()), b(sf["obs_ci_lower"].to_numpy()), b(sf["obs_ci_upper"].to_numpy())


def _judge(resp, r, ratio=1.0):
    """The judgement over the NOR (REPORT-LESSONS §1 rule 1): (met, deciding statistic)."""
    lo_, hi_, st_ = D.effective_acceptance(UO, resp)
    mean, plo, phi = (v / ratio for v in _pi(r, _NOR_C))
    if D.decision_statistic(resp) == "batch":
        return bool(phi.max() <= hi_), float(phi.max())
    return bool(mean.min() >= lo_), float(mean.min())


def _viral_par_lo(resp, r, factor="load_ph", n=81):
    """Lower edge of the worst-case NOR-propagated PAR of `factor` (viral clearance)."""
    claim = D.effective_acceptance(UO, resp)[0]
    others = [g for g in FS if g != factor]
    combos = list(itertools.product(*[[float(D.to_coded(UO, g, v)) for v in (P[g].nor[0], P[g].setpoint, P[g].nor[1])]
                                      for g in others]))
    xs = np.linspace(-1, 1, n)
    ok = []
    for x in xs:
        pts = pd.DataFrame([{factor: x, **dict(zip(others, c))} for c in combos])[FS]
        ok.append(_pi(r, pts)[0].min() >= claim)
    ok = np.array(ok)
    i = int(np.argmin(np.abs(xs - float(D.to_coded(UO, factor, P[factor].setpoint)))))
    assert ok[i]
    while i > 0 and ok[i - 1]:
        i -= 1
    return float(D.to_natural(UO, factor, xs[i]))


def _excluded(resp, r):
    """Grid points of the design-space grid this output alone excludes (viral clearance on the mean)."""
    claim = D.effective_acceptance(UO, resp)[0]
    return _pi(r, _CUBE)[0] < claim


def _max_upper(resp, r, ratio=1.0):
    """Highest single-run 95 % upper limit anywhere on the design-space grid."""
    return float((_pi(r, _CUBE)[2] / ratio).max())


_RAW = {r: (lambda d_: d_[d_[r].notna()].reset_index(drop=True))(D.rsm_data(UO, "all")) for r in CRIT_OUT}
SEL_R = {r: _refit(r, _RAW[r], FIT[r]["names"], FIT[r]["block"], FIT[r]["transform"] == "log") for r in CRIT_OUT}
for r in CRIT_OUT:                                   # the evaluator reproduces the engine
    assert _judge(r, SEL_R[r], OFF["offset"] if r == HCP else 1.0)[0] == D.nor_met(UO, r)
EXCL_SEL = {r: _excluded(r, SEL_R[r]) for r in (XM, MV)}
DS = D.design_space_grid(UO, n=DS_N)
DS_MEAN = D.design_space_grid(UO, n=DS_N, basis="mean")
assert np.isclose(DS["fraction"], 1 - (EXCL_SEL[XM] | EXCL_SEL[MV]).mean())
assert DS["binding"] == MV and DS["per_response"][HCP] == 0 and DS["per_response"][FRAG] == 0
PARLO = {r: _viral_par_lo(r, SEL_R[r]) for r in (XM, MV)}


def _near(resp):
    f = FIT[resp]
    d, y, blk = f["df"], f["df"][f["ycol"]].to_numpy(float), f["block"]
    res = sorted(((D.ad.aicc(y, D.ad.matrix(d, t, blk).to_numpy(float)), t) for t in D.ad.hierarchical_subsets(FS)),
                 key=lambda z: z[0])
    best = res[0][0]
    assert np.isclose(best, f["aicc"])
    return [(a - best, list(t)) for a, t in res if a - best <= 2.0]


NEAR = {r: _near(r) for r in CRIT_OUT}
NE_ROWS, NE_ALL_MET, NE_QUAL, NE_PARLO, NE_DSF = [], True, True, {XM: [], MV: []}, []
for r in CRIT_OUT:
    log = FIT[r]["transform"] == "log"
    for da, t in NEAR[r]:
        rr = _refit(r, _RAW[r], t, FIT[r]["block"], log)
        if r == HCP:
            met = {e: _judge(r, rr, OFF[e]) for e in ("offset", "lo", "hi")}
            ok = all(v[0] for v in met.values())
            NE_QUAL &= ok
            stat = met["offset"][1]
            extra = _max_upper(r, rr, OFF["lo"])
            assert extra <= D.effective_acceptance(UO, r)[1]
        else:
            ok, stat = _judge(r, rr)
            if r in (XM, MV):
                NE_PARLO[r].append(_viral_par_lo(r, rr))
                ex = {XM: EXCL_SEL[XM], MV: EXCL_SEL[MV]}
                ex[r] = _excluded(r, rr)
                NE_DSF.append(1 - (ex[XM] | ex[MV]).mean())
            else:
                assert _max_upper(r, rr) <= D.effective_acceptance(UO, r)[1]
        NE_ALL_MET &= ok
        NE_ROWS.append((r, da, t, ok, stat))
assert NE_ALL_MET and NE_QUAL
NE_N = {r: len(NEAR[r]) for r in CRIT_OUT}
NE_PARLO_MIN = {r: min(v) for r, v in NE_PARLO.items()}
NE_PARLO_MAX = {r: max(v) for r, v in NE_PARLO.items()}
NE_DSF_MIN, NE_DSF_MAX = min(NE_DSF), max(NE_DSF)
HCP_NE_AB = sum("load_ph:wash1_cond" in t for _, t in NEAR[HCP])
assert all({"load_ph", "wash1_cond"} <= set(t) for _, t in NEAR[HCP])
assert not any("wash1_cond:load" in t for _, t in NEAR[HCP])
XM_NE_AD = sum("load_ph:load" in t for _, t in NEAR[XM])
assert NE_N[XM] == 2 and XM_NE_AD == 1

DEL_ROWS = []
for r in RESP + [FRAG]:
    for run in RI[r]["over"]:
        dd = _RAW.get(r, (lambda d_: d_[d_[r].notna()].reset_index(drop=True))(D.rsm_data(UO, "all")))
        dd = dd[dd["run"] != run].reset_index(drop=True)
        sel = D.ad.select_model(dd, r, FS, D.TH)
        rr = {"factors": FS, "names": list(sel["terms"]), "quad": True, "block": bool(sel["block"]),
              "model": sel["model"], "log": sel["scale"] == "log"}
        cd = float(RI[r]["cook"][RI[r]["runs"].index(run)])
        if r in CRIT_OUT:
            if r == HCP:
                jj = {e: _judge(r, rr, OFF[e]) for e in ("offset", "lo", "hi")}
                ok, stat = all(v[0] for v in jj.values()), jj["offset"][1]
            else:
                ok, stat = _judge(r, rr)
            plo = _viral_par_lo(r, rr) if r in (XM, MV) else None
        else:
            ok, stat, plo = None, None, None
        dsf = None
        if r in (XM, MV):
            ex_ = {XM: EXCL_SEL[XM], MV: EXCL_SEL[MV]}
            ex_[r] = _excluded(r, rr)
            dsf = float(1 - (ex_[XM] | ex_[MV]).mean())
        elif r in (HCP, FRAG):
            assert _max_upper(r, rr, OFF["lo"] if r == HCP else 1.0) <= D.effective_acceptance(UO, r)[1]
        DEL_ROWS.append(dict(resp=r, run=int(run), cook=cd, lim=RI[r]["cook_limit"], flim=RI[r]["f_limit"], dsf=dsf,
                             terms=list(sel["terms"]), scale=sel["scale"], adequate=bool(sel["adequate"]),
                             same=list(sel["terms"]) == FIT[r]["names"] and sel["scale"] == ("log" if FIT[r]["transform"] == "log" else "raw"),
                             met=ok, stat=stat, parlo=plo))
DEL = pd.DataFrame(DEL_ROWS)
assert DEL.loc[DEL["met"].notna(), "met"].all()
DEL_CHANGED = DEL[~DEL["same"]]

# --- the verification of the platform worst case (host cell protein clearance) ----------
VER = D.iac_verification(UO).set_index("cqa")
VH = VER.loc["hcp"]
assert bool(VH["met"]) and bool(VH["widening_supported"]) and bool(VH["model_adequate"])
VALL = D.verification_all_runs()
VALL = VALL[VALL["step_key"] == UO].set_index("cqa").loc["hcp"]
VFULL = csv("iac_verification_full.csv")
VFULL = VFULL[VFULL["step_key"] == UO].set_index("cqa").loc["hcp"]
assert not bool(VFULL["model_adequate"]) and not bool(VFULL["widening_supported"])
PS = csv("process_summary.csv")
HCP_LOAD = float(PS.loc[PS["step"] == CFG.unit_op("cex").step, "hcp_out_ng_mg"].iloc[0])
_edge = RSM[(RSM[[f"coded_{f}" for f in FS]].abs() == 1).any(axis=1)]
EDGE_RUN = int(_edge.loc[_edge[HCP].idxmax(), "run"])
assert np.isclose(HCP_LOAD / float(_edge[HCP].max()), float(VH["observed_edge"]), rtol=1e-3)
assert float(VH["observed_edge"]) < float(VH["assumed"]) < float(VH["predicted_nor_bound95"])
RI_P = D.residual_influence(UO, HCP, runs="planned")
_cfg = _load_config()
_ps = csv("process_summary.csv")
_nf = D._nominal_fragments()
_base = D.rsm_data(UO, runs="planned", corrected=False)
_loo = []
for run in _base["run"]:
    o_ = _iac.verification(_cfg, {UO: _base[_base["run"] != run].reset_index(drop=True)}, _ps, _nf,
                           vi_feed_acidic=float("nan"))
    o_ = o_[(o_["step_key"] == UO) & (o_["cqa"] == "hcp")].iloc[0]
    _loo.append((int(run), float(o_["predicted_nor_bound95"]), bool(o_["widening_supported"])))
LOO = pd.DataFrame(_loo, columns=["run", "bound", "widen"])
assert LOO["widen"].all() and (LOO["bound"] > float(VH["assumed"])).all()
LOO_MIN = LOO.loc[LOO["bound"].idxmin()]
LOO_MAX = LOO.loc[LOO["bound"].idxmax()]
LOO_FLAG = {int(x): float(LOO.set_index("run").loc[int(x), "bound"]) for x in RI_P["over"]}
# the bound is a scale-down value: with the offset of the scale-down model (a ratio) it moves
B95 = float(VH["predicted_nor_bound95"])
B_EST, B_LO, B_HI = B95 * OFF["offset"], B95 * OFF["lo"], B95 * OFF["hi"]
assert B_EST > float(VH["assumed"]) > B_LO
IACALL = csv("iac.csv")
IACFULL = csv("iac_full.csv")


def _iac_hi(t, step):
    return float(t[(t["step_key"] == step) & (t["cqa"] == "hcp")]["iac_high"].iloc[0])


PA_HCP, CEX_HCP = _iac_hi(IACALL, "protein_a"), _iac_hi(IACALL, "cex")
PA_HCP0, CEX_HCP0 = _iac_hi(IACFULL, "protein_a"), _iac_hi(IACFULL, "cex")
CEX_HCP_FOLD = float(IACALL[(IACALL["step_key"] == "protein_a") & (IACALL["cqa"] == "hcp")]["downstream_fold"].iloc[0]) / B95
CA3 = D.ca3_criteria_sensitivity().set_index(["step_key", "response"])
QD_PA, QD_CEX = bool(CA3.loc[("protein_a", "pool_hcp_ng_mg"), "qualification_differs"]), bool(CA3.loc[("cex", HCP), "qualification_differs"])
assert QD_PA and QD_CEX
assert not CA3.loc[[(UO, r) for r in CRIT_OUT], "conclusion_differs"].any()
assert not CA3.loc[[(UO, r) for r in CRIT_OUT], "criterion_moved"].any()
POOS = D.p_oos().set_index("key")
CAP = cap.set_index("key")
N_MC = int(V["n_monte_carlo"])
POOS_UB = 1 - 0.05 ** (1 / N_MC)              # one-sided 95 % upper bound when no batch is outside
assert int(POOS.loc["hcp", "n_oos"]) == 0
HCP_LOQ, HCP_COV, HCP_PREC = DEV_SCALARS["amv_3012_loq"], DEV_SCALARS["amv_3012_coverage"], DEV_SCALARS["amv_3012_precision"]
HCP_COV_METHOD = str(METH.loc["AMV-3012", "coverage_method"])
# a CEX pool at its widened criterion needs this anion exchange clearance to reach 100 ng/mg
DS_HCP = D.effective_acceptance(UO, HCP)[1]
CEX_AT_PLATFORM = CEX_HCP / float(VH["assumed"])

# --- outputs against their criteria ------------------------------------------------------
NORMET = {r: D.nor_met(UO, r) for r in CRIT_OUT}
assert all(NORMET.values())
WC = {r: D.nor_worst_corner(UO, r) for r in CRIT_OUT}
NPL_HCP = D.nor_prediction_limit(UO, HCP, "upper")
NPL_FRAG = D.nor_prediction_limit(UO, FRAG, "upper")
MARGIN_HCP = DS_HCP / NPL_HCP

def _ttest(col, scale=1.0):
    lo_ = _u.loc[_u["value"] == FLOW_LO, col].to_numpy(float) * scale
    hi_ = _u.loc[_u["value"] == FLOW_HI, col].to_numpy(float) * scale
    t_, p_ = _sst.ttest_ind(hi_, lo_, equal_var=True)
    dfr = len(lo_) + len(hi_) - 2
    sp_ = np.sqrt(((len(lo_) - 1) * lo_.var(ddof=1) + (len(hi_) - 1) * hi_.var(ddof=1)) / dfr)
    hw = _sst.t.ppf(0.975, dfr) * sp_ * np.sqrt(1 / len(lo_) + 1 / len(hi_))
    dd_ = hi_.mean() - lo_.mean()
    return dict(lo=lo_, hi=hi_, diff=dd_, p=float(p_), ci=(dd_ - hw, dd_ + hw), df=dfr)
```

# Executive summary {.unnumbered}

This report presents the Stage 1 process characterization of the anion exchange step, Step 8 of the `{python} PRODUCT` drug substance process, for a commercial bioreactor scale of `{python} SCALE_L` L. The step is operated in flow-through mode and is the last chromatography step before virus filtration. It clears host cell protein, residual DNA, leached Protein A and virus. The register of critical quality attributes assigns to it the cumulative clearance of minute virus of mice (MVM), and it contributes a claim to the clearance of xenotropic murine leukaemia virus (XMuLV). The studies were run under the characterization plan PCP-008 in a scale-down model qualified under SOP-1001. They follow the lifecycle approach to process validation [@fda2011], ICH Q8(R2), Q9(R1) and Q11 [@ichq8; @ichq9; @ichq11], ICH Q5A(R2) for the viral clearance claims [@ichq5a] and the A-Mab case study [@amab2009]. This Version 2.0 is issued under the investigations INV-001 and INV-002.

Four parameters (load pH, Equil/Wash-1 conductivity, load conductivity and protein load) were studied in a screening design of `{python} n_scr` runs and a response-surface design of `{python} n_rsm` runs. In `{python} AUG_MONTH` the response-surface design was augmented by `{python} n_aug` runs, a number INV-002 calculated. Operating flow rate was assessed one factor at a time. The first execution of both designs ran on a deamidated load and was invalidated, and both designs were re-executed on a requalified load (study event DEV-008-01).

Each response-surface output was analysed by the model selection of INV-002 corrective action CA3, and every selected model meets the four adequacy criteria of the master plan PCMP-001 §7.2. Pool host cell protein is modelled on the log scale and depends on load pH and Equil/Wash-1 conductivity. The log reduction factors (LRFs) of both viruses depend on load pH and load conductivity. No effect of the parameters on step yield or on fragments was detected within the ranges studied. Every output with a criterion met its intermediate acceptance criterion at every combination of NOR low, set-point and NOR high, at manufacturing scale. The upper 95 % limit of a single run of pool host cell protein reached at most `{python} fx(NPL_HCP, 1)` ng/mg against `{python} HCP_CRIT`. At the least favourable combination the mean XMuLV LRF was `{python} fx(WC_MEAN[XM])` log10 against the step claim of `{python} CL_X` log10, and the mean MVM LRF `{python} fx(WC_MEAN[MV])` log10 against `{python} CL_M` log10.

The design space covers `{python} fx(100 * DSF, 1)` % of a grid over the characterized region and contains the whole NOR. It is drawn on the single-batch limit for the quality attributes and on the mean prediction for viral clearance, and MVM clearance bounds it where load pH is low and load conductivity high. Every proven acceptable range contains its NOR. For both viruses the NOR-propagated range of load pH ends inside the characterized range, `{python} fx(min(MARG.values()))` pH units below the lower end of the NOR. The scale-down model is qualified for pool host cell protein, the one compared output with a criterion at this step.

The host cell protein clearance of the step was verified against its platform worst case of `{python} PLAT`-fold. The one-sided 95 % prediction bound of a single batch is `{python} fx(B95)`-fold. It replaced the platform value and widened the host cell protein criteria of the Protein A pool and the cation exchange pool to `{python} f"{PA_HCP:,.0f}"` and `{python} f"{CEX_HCP:,.0f}"` ng/mg. The bound does not depend on a single run. It does depend on the model selection, because the plan's full quadratic model fails the limit on overfitting. It is also calculated from the scale-down results without the offset of the scale-down model, and with the offset at the unfavourable end of its 90 % interval it would be `{python} fx(B_LO)`-fold, below the platform value.

All five parameters were classified as well-controlled critical process parameters (WC-CPP). In the integrated process model of `{python} f"{N_MC:,}"` simulated batches, the cumulative MVM clearance has the lowest Cpk of the attributes this step sets or clears, `{python} CAP_TXT["lrv_mvm"]`, above the target of `{python} f"{CPK_TARGET:g}"`. No simulated batch fell outside any of their criteria. The record holds three study events from the execution (DEV-008-01 to DEV-008-03) and three discrepancies from the plan, namely the augmentation, the model selection and a flow-rate study run without its centre run (`{python} PD_AUG` to `{python} PD_FLOW`). The results roll up into the master report PCMR-001, which consolidates the cumulative viral clearance claim.

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

## Product and unit operation {#sec-product}

A-Mab is a humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody whose primary mechanism of action is antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity [@amab2009]. It is purified on the platform train of Protein A capture, low-pH viral inactivation, cation exchange, anion exchange, virus filtration and UF/DF. The process is being transferred from the development site in `{python} SENDING_LOCATION` to the commercial drug substance site in `{python} RECEIVING_LOCATION` under the Process Transfer Plan PTP-001. The commercial process runs at a bioreactor scale of `{python} SCALE_L` L.

Anion exchange chromatography is Step 8 of the train. The resin carries a quaternary amine ligand with a fixed positive charge. At the load pH the antibody carries a net positive charge and passes through the bed, while species that carry a net negative charge bind. These are residual DNA, the acidic part of the host cell protein population, leached Protein A and virus particles. The column is equilibrated, loaded with the cation exchange pool adjusted to its target pH and conductivity, and chased with the first wash buffer. The pool is collected from the start of the load to the end of the chase. The step processes the cation exchange pool of a single batch at commercial scale (PCP-008 §1).

The register of critical quality attributes assigns the cumulative MVM clearance to this step (@tbl-cqa). The step also contributes a modular XMuLV clearance claim. It clears host cell protein, residual DNA and leached Protein A, which are formed upstream and cleared by more than one step, and fragments are judged in its pool. @tbl-related lists the documents this report rests on and those that use it.

## Objectives {#sec-objectives}

The study had six objectives, as PCP-008 §2 states them:

1. Quantify the effect of each studied parameter on pool host cell protein, on the LRFs of XMuLV and MVM, and on step yield, over the ranges of @tbl-params, and the effect of each multivariate parameter on fragments.
2. Define the multivariate operating region within which every governed quality attribute meets its criterion, a quality attribute on the single-batch limit and viral clearance on its mean prediction, as PCMP-001 Version 2.0 draws its design space, and state where the boundary of that region lies.
3. Establish a proven acceptable range for each parameter and each attribute it governs, and confirm that the NOR falls inside it.
4. Classify each parameter under the parameter classification procedure SOP-4001 from the effects demonstrated in the study and from the capability with which the parameter can be held.
5. Determine whether the step meets its platform claims for both model viruses at the worst case within the NOR, and justify the Stage 2 ranges and this step's part of the control strategy.
6. Verify the host cell protein clearance of this step against its platform worst case, `{python} PLAT`-fold, on which the host cell protein criteria of the upstream steps rely.

## Regulatory and scientific basis {#sec-regulatory}

The study is part of Stage 1, process design, of the lifecycle approach to process validation [@fda2011]. It follows the enhanced approach of ICH Q8(R2) and ICH Q11 [@ichq8; @ichq11]. Prior knowledge and risk assessment identify the parameters that may affect the critical quality attributes, and designed studies measure and bound those effects. Criticality is treated as a continuum, as ICH Q8(R2) describes it, and the risk assessment follows ICH Q9(R1) [@ichq9]. The viral clearance of this step is a modular claim under ICH Q5A(R2) [@ichq5a]. Each claimed step is studied in its own spiking model, and the cumulative claim is consolidated in PCMR-001. The process model, the attribute framework and the risk method come from the A-Mab case study [@amab2009].

This report states its results against PCP-008 Version 2.0 and the master plan PCMP-001 Version 2.0. The procedures and method validations it cites are listed in @tbl-sops.

# Prior knowledge and quality risk basis {#sec-prior}

## Platform and prior-product knowledge {#sec-platform}

The platform anion exchange step has been used to manufacture three earlier humanized IgG1 antibodies, X-Mab, Y-Mab and Z-Mab, and to supply A-Mab clinical studies [@amab2009]. That experience established the mode of operation, the buffer system and the clearance the step delivers. It also gave the two platform worst cases of this step on which the criteria of the upstream steps rely, a host cell protein clearance of at least `{python} PLAT`-fold and a leached Protein A clearance of at least `{python} f"{LPA_PLAT:g}"`-fold (PCMP-001 §7.3). The platform claims of the step are `{python} CL_X` log10 for XMuLV and `{python} CL_M` log10 for MVM (PCMP-001 §7.4). Characterization of A-Mab therefore confirms and bounds known behaviour.

Whether an impurity binds depends on its net charge at the load pH and on how strongly the ionic strength of the buffer shields that charge. A higher load pH moves more of the host cell protein population below its isoelectric point and makes the acidic impurities and the virus particles more negative, so they bind more strongly. Load pH is therefore expected to lower pool host cell protein and to raise both LRFs. The antibody, whose isoelectric point lies well above the load pH, stays positively charged and passes through. Step yield is therefore not expected to depend on load pH within the range studied.

A higher conductivity of the equilibration and first wash buffer shields the electrostatic interaction and lets weakly bound host cell protein and virus particles through. Equil/Wash-1 conductivity is therefore expected to raise pool host cell protein and to lower both LRFs. Load conductivity acts by the same shielding during the load and is expected to act in the same directions. Load pH and the conductivities act on the same binding equilibrium from opposite sides. For this reason PCP-008 §4.1 expected the effect of Equil/Wash-1 conductivity on host cell protein to depend on load pH.

Protein load sets the impurity mass applied per litre of resin. Pool host cell protein is expressed per milligram of antibody, so a higher load raises it only where the bound impurity approaches the capacity of the ligand. Within the range studied the impurity mass is expected to stay below that capacity, and no effect of protein load is expected. Operating flow rate sets the residence time in the bed. Binding of the small, highly charged impurities is fast, so only a small effect is expected. Virus particles diffuse slowly to the ligand and are the most likely to show an effect at the shortest residence time.

Residual DNA is a polyanion at every pH the step could run at and binds the ligand strongly. Its clearance is expected to be large and robust to the parameters. Leached Protein A is acidic and binds while the antibody passes through. Fragments are expected to leave the step at the level at which they enter it, because on the platform no step after cation exchange changes the fragment level (PCMP-001 §7.3). This study measured fragments in the pool only, so that expectation was not tested here.

For both model viruses, clearance is expected to fall as the load pH drops toward the point at which the particle surface loses its negative charge, and as conductivity rises. The XMuLV claim of this step is orthogonal to that of low-pH inactivation, which acts on the viral envelope and not on the surface charge. MVM is not inactivated by low pH, so this step and the virus filter carry the whole MVM claim (PCMP-001 §7.4).

@tbl-cqa lists the attributes to which the step contributes, with their drug substance criteria and their criticality. Criticality was assigned with Tool #1 of the A-Mab case study, from the impact of each attribute on safety and efficacy and the uncertainty in that impact [@amab2009]. Attributes of high and very high criticality are critical. The two viral clearance attributes carry very high criticality by rule, because a viral contamination would harm the patient directly (PCMP-001 §3).

The criteria that apply to the outputs of this step are the intermediate acceptance criteria of @sec-par-basis. For pool host cell protein and fragments they equal the drug substance criteria, and for viral clearance they are the claims of this step. The cumulative requirements of `{python} REQ_X` log10 for XMuLV and `{python} REQ_M` log10 for MVM are met by the sum of the claims of several steps. This step contributes one of three claims for XMuLV and one of two for MVM. Residual DNA and leached Protein A have no intermediate acceptance criterion at this step and were monitored, not modelled (PCP-008 §5.4). ## Risk-based prioritization and parameter selection {#sec-risk}

The risk assessment RA-001 ranked each parameter on its potential impact on a critical quality attribute and on its potential to interact with other parameters. Parameters ranked high on both were assigned to the designed studies, and parameters ranked high on impact but low on interaction to a univariate assessment. For this step, `{python} len(FS)` parameters went to the designs and `{python} len(UNI)` to a univariate assessment (@tbl-params). Load pH, Equil/Wash-1 conductivity and load conductivity ranked highest, because together they set how strongly an acidic host cell protein binds. Protein load was included because the impurity mass loaded onto the column scales with it and the ligand has a finite capacity. Operating flow rate was assessed one factor at a time, because binding of the small, highly charged impurities is fast relative to the residence time at every flow rate in the range.

The load is the cation exchange pool, whose attributes are set by the preceding step and characterized under PCP-007. This study varied the parameters of the anion exchange step and did not vary the quality of its load.

# Materials and methods {#sec-methods}

## Scale-down model and its qualification {#sec-sdm}

The studies were executed on a scale-down model of the commercial anion exchange column, qualified under SOP-1001 and operated under SOP-2011. The model keeps the bed height, the linear flow velocity, the protein load in grams of antibody per litre of resin, and the equilibration, load, wash and chase volumes in column volumes. Scaling on these variables holds the residence time and the impurity mass per unit of ligand equal to those of the commercial step. The resin, the buffers and the packing method are the same as at commercial scale.

The qualification study S-AEX-SDM (`{python} win("S-AEX-SDM")`) compared `{python} OFF["n_sd"]` scale-down runs at set-point with `{python} OFF["n_m"]` batches at manufacturing scale. It ended before the first execution of the designs began on `{python} W["S-AEX-SUP"][0]`, as PCP-008 §5.1 requires. It compared step yield, pool host cell protein, column efficiency and peak asymmetry. It also measured residual DNA and leached Protein A in the pools, and every one of those results was below the limit of quantitation (LOQ) at both scales, so no offset could be estimated for either. The pressure across the bed, which PCP-008 §5.1 lists among the compared outputs, was not measured.

The offset of an output is the mean of the scale-down runs minus the mean of the manufacturing batches, with its two-sided 90 % confidence interval, each end of which is a one-sided 95 % bound (PCMP-001 §7.1). Pool host cell protein is modelled on the log scale (@sec-stats). Its offset is therefore the ratio of the geometric means, and a scale-down value is divided by it. The model is qualified for an output when the conclusion against its criterion over the NOR is the same with the offset at either end of its interval. That conclusion is whether the output meets its criterion at every combination of NOR low, set-point and NOR high of the four multivariate parameters.

```{python}
#| output: asis
T.sdm_offsets(["aex"]).show()
```

@tbl-sdm-offsets gives the offsets. Pool host cell protein, the only compared output with a criterion at this step, has a ratio of `{python} fx(OFF["offset"], 3)` (90 % interval `{python} fx(OFF["lo"], 3)` to `{python} fx(OFF["hi"], 3)`). Its criterion is met over the NOR with the offset at its estimate and at both ends of the interval, so the scale-down model is qualified for pool host cell protein. The other compared outputs have no criterion at this step, and their offsets are recorded. The scale-down column gave fewer plates per metre than the manufacturing columns, and the 90 % interval of that difference excludes zero. No conclusion of this report depends on column efficiency.

The qualification did not compare fragments or viral clearance at the two scales. Their offset is unknown, not zero, and they are judged as the scale-down model gives them (PCMP-001 §7.1). For fragments, the representativeness rests on the expectation of @sec-platform that the step does not change the fragment level of its load. For viral clearance it rests on the spiking model. The spiking runs were made in the same scale-down model as a small-scale spiking study [@ichq5a]. PCP-008 §5.1 required a qualification of the spiking model, showing that the spiked load matched the unspiked load in protein concentration, pH and conductivity and that the spike volume stayed below the fraction at which those attributes move. The record of this study holds no result of that qualification.

The centre points of each design were separate runs of the step. Their replicates estimate pure error, against which lack of fit is tested (@sec-centre).

## Operation {#sec-operation}

The step was operated as at commercial scale, under SOP-2011. The column was equilibrated with the equilibration buffer, loaded with the cation exchange pool adjusted to the target pH and conductivity of the run, and chased with the first wash buffer. The pool was collected from the start of the load to the end of the chase, which a trailing-edge UV set-point ends (@sec-dev02). Resin, buffers and column packing are controlled to platform specification under SOP-2008 and the site buffer procedure (PCP-008 §5.2), and they are not characterized here.

The re-executed screening and response-surface designs ran on one requalified load lot, LOT-CEX-8851, so the comparison of a second load lot that PCP-008 §6.3 requires did not arise. The first, invalidated execution ran on lot LOT-CEX-8842 (@sec-dev01). The record does not name the load lot of the augmentation runs of `{python} AUG_MONTH`. Lot LOT-CEX-8851 had expired on `{python} LOTS.loc["LOT-CEX-8851", "expiry"]`, before the augmentation began, and the record holds no comparison of the augmentation load with it. The block term of the models estimates a shift between the planned runs and the augmentation runs (@sec-reeval). The record of these studies does not name the chromatography system on which they ran, so its calibration status cannot be shown for them, as PCP-008 §11 also states.

## Analytical methods {#sec-analytical}

Every response was measured by a validated method (@tbl-sops). Pool host cell protein was measured by ELISA (AMV-3012) and is reported in nanograms per milligram of antibody. Residual DNA was measured by qPCR (AMV-3014) and leached Protein A by ELISA (AMV-3016). The infectivity of XMuLV was measured by TCID50 (AMV-3017) and that of MVM by TCID50 with a qPCR confirmation (AMV-3018). The charge variant profile of the load was measured by icIEF (AMV-3013). Fragments were measured by nrCE-SDS (AMV-3020, under SOP-3015), the method that AMD-001 set for every study that measures fragments, at every step, from `{python} AMD["date"]` (PCMP-001 §7.8). The re-executed designs ran after that date and measured fragments by nrCE-SDS, and the invalidated first execution had measured them by SEC (@tbl-methods-by-study). Aggregate was not a response of the designs, because PCMP-001 sets no aggregate criterion at this step.

The precision of each method bounds the smallest effect the study can resolve, because method variability enters the residual of each model and is not separated from process variability (Appendix D). The repeatability of the infectivity assays is `{python} f"{REP_X:g}"` log10 for XMuLV and `{python} f"{REP_M:g}"` log10 for MVM, and the precision of the host cell protein ELISA is `{python} f"{HCP_PREC:g}"` % of the level.

## Sampling plan {#sec-sampling}

Samples were taken from the load and the flow-through pool of every run, and the pool sample carries the responses. The screening design included `{python} n_cp_scr` centre points and the response-surface design `{python} n_cp_rsm`, each a separate run of the step. Residual DNA and leached Protein A were measured in the load and the pool of every planned response-surface run and in the pools of the qualification runs. The augmentation runs measured pool host cell protein, step yield and fragments. They measured no viral clearance, because INV-002 spiked no virus in an augmentation, and no residual DNA or leached Protein A.

Viral clearance runs were sampled at the spiked load and at the pool. Each LRF is the log10 ratio of the total infectivity in the spiked load to that in the pool (PCP-008 §5.4) [@ichq5a]. PCP-008 §5.4 also required cytotoxicity and interference controls for each matrix, and the detection limit of the assay with any result that reached it. The record of this study holds the LRFs and not those controls.

## Statistical methods {#sec-stats}

### Coding and the screening model

Each multivariate parameter was coded so that the ends of its characterized range are −1 and +1 and its middle is 0. For load pH, Equil/Wash-1 conductivity and load conductivity the middle of the range is the set-point. For protein load the middle is `{python} qv("load", MID["load"])`, and the set-point is `{python} SPS["load"]`.

The screening data were fitted by ordinary least squares with every main effect and every two-factor interaction in coded units. An effect is twice the coded coefficient, which is the change in the response across the characterized range. A term is significant when its p-value is below `{python} f"{ALPHA:g}"` (PCMP-001 §6.2). The screening model identifies effects. It is not the predictive model, and no range is derived from it.

### The response-surface models and their selection

PCP-008 planned the full quadratic model in the four multivariate parameters. Each output was instead analysed by the model selection of INV-002 corrective action CA3 [@montgomery2017]. This report records that change as the discrepancy `{python} PD_SEL` (@sec-discrepancies). The selection has four parts.

1. The scale. The Box-Cox profile of the full quadratic model [@boxcox1964] chooses the log scale where its 95 % interval for λ contains 0 and excludes 1, and the raw scale otherwise.
2. The model. Among all hierarchical submodels of the full quadratic, the one with the lowest AICc is selected. A hierarchical submodel contains an interaction only with both its main effects and a square only with its main effect. For four parameters there are `{python} f"{N_SUBSETS:,}"` candidates, and every one was fitted.
3. The block. Where the design has a second block, the augmentation runs, a block term is kept in every candidate.
4. The check. The selected model is judged against the four adequacy criteria of PCMP-001 §7.2 given below.

AICc is Akaike's information criterion with the small-sample correction [@hurvich1989; @burnham2002]. It estimates how well a model would predict new runs, and it penalises every estimated coefficient. Its correction raises that penalty when the runs are few for the number of terms, as they are in these designs, so that the criterion does not favour too many terms. Here the residual variance is counted as one of the estimated parameters. This report counts the terms of a model without the intercept and the block term.

The search is exhaustive. A stepwise search changes one term at a time and stops when no single change lowers AICc, so it stops where only a combination of changes would lower AICc further. Across the outputs of the campaign, a backward stepwise search would have stopped at a worse model for `{python} n_bw_worse` of `{python} n_sc` outputs and a forward search for `{python} n_fw_worse` (INV-002). At this step a forward search would have stopped at a worse model for XMuLV, and a backward search for MVM and for fragments. INV-002 had first refitted the failing models it did not augment by backward elimination on p-values, on the raw scale (its corrective action CA2). Corrective action CA3, adopted on `{python} MA["selection_adopted"]`, replaced that refit with the selection described here.

Where other models lie within 2 AICc units of the selected one, they are near-equivalent. The selected model decides, and the near-equivalent models are reported as a sensitivity (@sec-near). A feature that only some of them carry is not treated as an established effect.

### The log scale

Pool host cell protein is the one output modelled on the log scale. Its Box-Cox λ is `{python} fx(BC["lambda"])`, with a 95 % interval from `{python} fx(BC["lo"])` to `{python} fx(BC["hi"])`, which contains 0 and excludes 1. On the log scale the model is $\ln y = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 x_2 + \dots + e$. Transformed back it is $y = e^{b_0} \cdot e^{b_1 x_1} \cdot e^{b_2 x_2} \cdots e^{e}$. Each parameter therefore multiplies the output by a fixed factor, $e^{b}$ per coded unit and $e^{2b}$ from the low to the high end of its range. The error of a single run multiplies it too, so its size in ng/mg grows with the level.

Two properties of the step and the assay make this form likely. A purification step removes a share of what is present, so a parameter changes the share and not a fixed amount. The precision of the host cell protein ELISA is a percentage of the level (`{python} f"{HCP_PREC:g}"` %), so the scatter of the results grows with the level. Least squares, and the t-tests, F-tests and prediction intervals built on it, assume residuals that are independent and normally distributed, with mean zero and the same variance over the whole range studied. With the selected terms fitted on the raw scale, the residual standard deviation is `{python} fx(raw_sd_lo)` ng/mg in the lower half of the predictions and `{python} fx(raw_sd_hi)` ng/mg in the upper half. On the log scale the two halves give `{python} fx(log_sd_lo, 3)` and `{python} fx(log_sd_hi, 3)`, about the same.

The criterion stays in its own unit, ng/mg, and the effects are fold changes. The scale-down offset is a ratio of geometric means (@sec-sdm). A prediction interval is calculated on the log scale and transformed back. It keeps its 95 % coverage, because the probability that $\ln y$ lies between two values is the probability that $y$ lies between their antilogs, and on the log scale the assumption of constant variance holds. The interval is asymmetric. At the least favourable combination within the NOR the predicted value is `{python} fx(WC[HCP]["predicted"], 1)` ng/mg at manufacturing scale, and the 95 % interval of a single run runs from `{python} fx(WC[HCP]["pi_low"], 1)` to `{python} fx(WC[HCP]["pi_high"], 1)` ng/mg, `{python} fx(WC[HCP]["pi_high"] - WC[HCP]["predicted"], 1)` above it and `{python} fx(WC[HCP]["predicted"] - WC[HCP]["pi_low"], 1)` below. The predicted value is the median of the output, its geometric mean, and not its arithmetic mean. The upper prediction limit, which decides against an upper criterion, is not affected by that. Near an upper criterion, where the level is high, a raw-scale model would understate the scatter, because its residual standard deviation is pooled over all levels.

### Model adequacy

PCMP-001 §7.2 sets four criteria for a model to be adequate for prediction:

1. The model F-test is significant at α = `{python} f"{ALPHA:g}"`. A model with no term has no F-test, and the criterion does not apply to it.
2. Lack of fit against pure error is not significant at α = `{python} f"{float(TH['lof_alpha']):g}"`.
3. Predicted R² falls short of R² by no more than `{python} fx(GAPMAX)`, the limit on overfitting.
4. The residuals show no pattern against the predicted values or the run order, and no single run dominates the fit.

The fourth criterion was tested as every Version 2.0 plan states it. The absolute residuals were regressed on the predicted values, and the residuals on the order of execution, each at α = `{python} f"{float(TH['residual_alpha']):g}"`. The runs of the second block continue the order of the first. A run with a Cook's distance above `{python} COOK_K`/n, where n is the number of runs, was examined by deleting it and repeating the judgement over the NOR. The model fails the criterion only where a run's Cook's distance exceeds the median of the F distribution with p and n − p degrees of freedom, where p is the number of estimated coefficients, the intercept and the block included. Each model is reported with R², adjusted R² and predicted R², the last computed from the prediction error sum of squares [@montgomery2017].

### Judgement over the NOR

A quality attribute is judged on a single batch, because its criterion applies to each batch. At every combination of NOR low, set-point and NOR high of the four multivariate parameters (`{python} n_nor` combinations), the exact 95 % prediction interval of a single run is computed from the selected model, with the coefficient and residual uncertainty. The interval is two-sided, so its upper end is a one-sided 97.5 % limit. A quality attribute meets its criterion over the NOR when every interval lies within it at manufacturing scale. Viral clearance is judged on the mean predicted LRF at the least favourable of the `{python} n_nor` combinations, because viral clearance is validated at worst-case conditions (PCMP-001 §6.4). Its single-run limit is given for information only. Pool host cell protein is divided by its offset before it is judged. Fragments and viral clearance have no offset and are judged as the scale-down model gives them.

### Proven acceptable ranges and the design space

Two analyses were run for each pair of a parameter and an attribute with a criterion (PCMP-001 §6.4). The first, in the column headed "PAR (set-point)", is a univariate range over which the mean prediction meets the criterion, scanned across the characterized range. The second, the NOR-propagated analysis, scans the parameter over `{python} D.PAR_GRID` grid points while the other parameters vary within their NORs. For a quality attribute, each other parameter is drawn `{python} f"{D.PAR_MC_N:,}"` times from a normal distribution centred on its set-point, with a standard deviation of one sixth of the width of its NOR, clipped to the characterized range. Each draw carries the model residual and the uncertainty of the coefficients, and the range is where the 97.5th percentile of the simulated batches stays within an upper criterion. For viral clearance the other parameters are set to each of their `{python} N_COMB` combinations of NOR low, set-point and NOR high, and the range is where the lowest mean prediction meets the claim. A range is reported only where it is contiguous and contains the set-point, and only from an adequate model. The simulation uses a fixed seed (`{python} D.PAR_SEED`). The NOR-propagated range is the one that supports a claim.

The design space is drawn on a grid of `{python} DS_N` levels per parameter across the characterized range (`{python} f"{DS['n_points']:,}"` points). A grid point lies inside when the 95 % prediction interval of a single run lies within the criterion for each quality attribute and the mean prediction meets the claim for each viral clearance output (PCMP-001 §6.2).

### Capability and other comparisons

Capability at commercial scale is estimated from the integrated process model of the train (PCMP-001 §6.5). The model runs `{python} f"{N_MC:,}"` simulated batches through every step, with each process parameter drawn as in the NOR-propagated analysis. It reports Cpk against each drug substance criterion and the probability that the drug substance is out of specification.

PCP-008 §7 sets no numerical threshold for an effect of flow rate or for an effect attributed to the infectivity assay, and it leaves the approach to this report. An effect of flow rate on pool host cell protein or step yield was tested by a two-sided t-test of the difference between the two ends of the range at α = `{python} f"{ALPHA:g}"`, the level PCMP-001 sets for model terms, and the difference is given with its 95 % confidence interval. A spiked run was compared with the claim and with the 95 % prediction interval of a single run at the set-point from the response-surface model. An apparent effect on an LRF no larger than the repeatability of its infectivity assay is attributed to the assay.

## Factors, ranges and the knowledge space {#sec-factors}

@tbl-params lists the parameters with their set-points, NORs and characterized ranges, the study type RA-001 assigned and the letter code of each multivariate parameter. The characterized range is wider than the NOR at both ends for every parameter. The edge of the operating region therefore lies inside the data, and a proven acceptable range is claimed only over settings that were run [@amab2009].

```{python}
#| output: asis
_rp = report_params(UO)
_rows = []
for k in list(FS) + UNI:
    p = P[k]
    _rows.append(["Designed experiments" if k in FS else "One factor at a time", LET.get(k, "–"), p.name,
                  p.unit, f"{p.setpoint:g}", f"{p.nor[0]:g}–{p.nor[1]:g}", f"{p.prange[0]:g}–{p.prange[1]:g}"])
_df_params = pd.DataFrame(_rows, columns=["Study type", "Code", "Parameter", "Unit", "Set-point", "NOR",
                                          "Characterized\nrange"])
_al_params = ["P{2.6cm}", "c", "P{3.6cm}", "l", "r", "r", "r"]
T.frame(_df_params, "Parameters, ranges and study type for the anion exchange characterization.", "tbl-params", merge=["Study type"], align=_al_params, size="footnotesize").show()
```

The load pH range lies below the pH at which a fraction of the antibody would begin to bind and yield would fall. The range of Equil/Wash-1 conductivity reflects the spread that buffer preparation and column equilibration can produce, and the range of load conductivity reflects what the preceding step delivers (PCP-008 §6.1). The centre points of both designs, and the axial runs of the response-surface design on every parameter they do not vary, sit at coded 0, the middle of each characterized range (@sec-stats). For protein load that is `{python} qv("load", MID["load"])`, below the set-point of `{python} SPS["load"]`, because the characterized range of protein load extends further below its set-point than above it.

## Screening design {#sec-screening-design}

The four multivariate parameters were studied in a two-level full factorial design of `{python} n_fact` runs with `{python} n_cp_scr` centre points, `{python} n_scr` runs in all (study S-AEX-SCR, `{python} win("S-AEX-SCR")`). A full factorial in four parameters estimates every main effect and every two-factor interaction without confounding, which the expected interaction of load pH and Equil/Wash-1 conductivity requires. The centre points estimate pure error and give a test for curvature. The runs were executed in randomized order on load lot LOT-CEX-8851 (Appendix A).

## Response-surface design {#sec-rsm-design}

The same parameters were studied in a face-centred central composite design of `{python} n_rsm` runs (study S-AEX-RSM, `{python} win("S-AEX-RSM")`), on the same load lot. The design adds `{python} n_axial` axial runs at the faces of the cube to the `{python} n_fact` factorial runs and `{python} n_cp_rsm` centre points, so every run lies inside the characterized range. Its quadratic terms allow for clearance that rises more steeply over part of the load pH range (Appendix B).

In `{python} AUG_MONTH` the design was augmented by `{python} n_aug` runs in a D-optimal augmentation [@fedorov1972], study `{python} AUG_ID` (`{python} win(AUG_ID)`), executed as a second block and numbered `{python} aug_first` to `{python} aug_last`. INV-002 decided its rule on `{python} MA["decided"]`, before any new run. It calculated the number of runs as the smallest augmentation that gives a probability of at least `{python} f"{float(MA['assurance']):.2f}"` that the plan's full quadratic model of pool host cell protein meets PCMP-001 §7.2. This report cites that number and does not recalculate it. The plan did not foresee the augmentation, and it is recorded as the discrepancy `{python} PD_AUG` (@sec-discrepancies).

## Univariate assessment {#sec-uni-design}

Operating flow rate was assessed one factor at a time, with the other parameters at their set-points as PCP-008 §6.4 sets (study S-AEX-UNI, `{python} win("S-AEX-UNI")`). Each end of its characterized range, `{python} f"{FLOW_LO:g}"` and `{python} qv("flow", FLOW_HI)`, was run in duplicate, and pool host cell protein and step yield were measured on each run. One spiked run at the upper end, the shortest residence time, measured the LRFs of both viruses. PCP-008 §6.4 planned the low, the centre and the high setting. No run was made at the centre, and the qualification runs at set-point serve as the reference (`{python} PD_FLOW`). A univariate assessment cannot resolve an interaction between flow rate and another parameter. Its claims therefore rest on the assumption that the effect of flow rate does not depend on where the other parameters sit.

# Results {#sec-results}

## Centre-point performance and reproducibility {#sec-centre}

@tbl-centre gives the mean and the spread of the centre points of both designs. Pool host cell protein is the least precise output in relative terms. Its coefficient of variation in the response-surface design is `{python} fx(CCV_R.loc[D.RESP_LABEL[HCP], "%CV"], 1)` %, against a precision of the ELISA of `{python} f"{HCP_PREC:g}"` %. The standard deviations of the LRFs at the centre point, `{python} fx(CCV_R.loc[D.RESP_LABEL[XM], "SD"], 3)` log10 for XMuLV and `{python} fx(CCV_R.loc[D.RESP_LABEL[MV], "SD"], 3)` log10 for MVM, compare with a repeatability of the infectivity assays of `{python} f"{REP_X:g}"` and `{python} f"{REP_M:g}"` log10. These replicates are the pure error against which lack of fit is tested.

```{python}
#| output: asis
_rows = []
for design, kind, df_ in (("Screening", "screening", SCR), ("Response surface", "rsm", RSM)):
    cv = D.center_cv_df(UO, kind).set_index("Response")
    cen = df_[df_["run_type"] == "center"]
    for r in RESP + [FRAG]:
        if r == FRAG:
            v = cen[FRAG]
            mean, sd, n = float(v.mean()), float(v.std(ddof=1)), len(v)
        else:
            row = cv.loc[D.RESP_LABEL[r]]
            mean, sd, n = float(row["Mean"]), float(row["SD"]), int(row["n"])
        k = 100.0 if r == YLD else 1.0
        nd = 1 if r in (HCP, YLD) else (2 if r in (XM, MV, FRAG) else 2)
        cvs = "n.a.^a)^" if r in (XM, MV) else fx(100 * sd / mean, 1)
        _rows.append([design, f"{RL[r]} ({RU[r]})", str(n), fx(mean * k, nd), fx(sd * k, 3 if r != HCP else 2), cvs])
_df_centre = pd.DataFrame(_rows, columns=["Design", "Output", "Centre\nruns", "Mean", "SD", "CV (%)"])
_nt_centre = [("a)", "Not given for a log reduction factor, which is already on a log scale."),
              ("", "SD, standard deviation. CV, coefficient of variation.")]
_al_centre = ["P{2.6cm}", "P{4.6cm}", "c", "r", "r", "r"]
T.frame(_df_centre, "Centre-point reproducibility of the anion exchange designs.", "tbl-centre", merge=["Design"], align=_al_centre, size="footnotesize", notes=_nt_centre, notes_per_row=True).show()
```

## Screening: factor effects {#sec-screening}

@tbl-screening summarises the screening models and gives the terms significant at `{python} f"{ALPHA:g}"`. Load pH and Equil/Wash-1 conductivity acted on pool host cell protein in opposite directions, with effects of `{python} fx(SE[HCP].loc["A", "Effect"], 1)` and +`{python} fx(SE[HCP].loc["B", "Effect"], 1)` ng/mg across their ranges, and their interaction was significant (`{python} fx(SE[HCP].loc["AB", "Effect"], 1)` ng/mg). Load pH raised both LRFs and load conductivity lowered them. No term was significant for step yield. For fragments the interaction of load pH and protein load was significant (`{python} fx(SE[FRAG].loc["AD", "Effect"], 3)` percentage points, `{python} pe(SE[FRAG].loc["AD", "p-value"])`) in a model whose F-test was not significant (`{python} pe(SFIT[FRAG]["p"])`). The full effect tables are in Appendix C.

```{python}
#| output: asis
_lg = {v: k for k, v in LET.items()}
_rows = []
for r in RESP + [FRAG]:
    f_ = SFIT[r]
    s_ = SIG[r]
    k = 100.0 if r == YLD else 1.0
    terms = ", ".join(f"{t} ({'+' if e > 0 else ''}{fx(e * k, 1 if r == HCP else 2)})" for t, e in zip(s_["Term"], s_["Effect"])) or "none"
    _rows.append([f"{RL[r]} ({RU[r]})", fx(f_["R2"]), fx(f_["adjR2"]), fx(f_["predR2"]), fp(f_["p"]), fp(f_["p_lof"]), terms])
_df_scr = pd.DataFrame(_rows, columns=["Output", "R²", "Adj. R²", "Pred. R²", "Model p", "Lack of\nfit p",
                                       "Terms significant at 0.05\n(effect across the range)"])
_nt_scr = [("", "A, load pH. B, Equil/Wash-1 conductivity. C, load conductivity. D, protein load. "
                "An effect is the change in the output, in its unit, from the low to the high end of the "
                "characterized range of the parameter.")]
_al_scr = ["P{3.8cm}", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "P{4.2cm}"]
T.frame(_df_scr, "Screening models of the anion exchange outputs.", "tbl-screening", align=_al_scr, size="footnotesize", notes=_nt_scr, notes_per_row=True).show()
```

The directions agree with the expectations of @sec-platform for load pH and Equil/Wash-1 conductivity on host cell protein, and for load pH and load conductivity on both viruses. No effect of load conductivity on host cell protein and no effect of Equil/Wash-1 conductivity on either virus was detected, although @sec-platform expected both. The screening models of `{python} join_and([resp_full(r) for r in SCR_NEG_PRED])` have a negative predicted R², so they do not predict. This type of design identifies effects but cannot fit curvature, and the response-surface model gives the magnitudes.

Pool host cell protein is modelled on the log scale on all `{python} FIT[HCP]["n"]` runs, with load pH, Equil/Wash-1 conductivity and a block term. The XMuLV LRF is modelled on the raw scale on the `{python} FIT[XM]["n"]` planned runs, with load pH, load conductivity, protein load and the interaction of load pH and protein load. The MVM LRF is modelled on the raw scale with load pH and load conductivity. The selected models of step yield and fragments contain no term besides the block, so no dependence of either output on the parameters was detected within the ranges studied, at the precision of the runs. These two models have no F-test, and the first criterion does not apply to them.

The residual regressions found no trend for any output. Cook's distance flagged at least one run in every model except that of MVM, and no run exceeded the median of the F distribution, so no model fails the fourth criterion (@sec-influence).

```{python}
        _rows.append([RL[r], x["Source"].strip(), fx(x["Sum sq."], 4), str(int(x["df"])), fx(x["Mean sq."], 4),
                      "" if pd.isna(x["F"]) else fx(x["F"], 2), "" if pd.isna(x["p-value"]) else fp(x["p-value"])])
_df_anova = pd.DataFrame(_rows, columns=["Output", "Source", "Sum of\nsquares", "df", "Mean\nsquare", "F", "p"])
_nt_anova = [("", "The residual divides into lack of fit and pure error from the centre points. Pool host cell "
                  "protein on the natural log scale.")]
_al_anova = ["P{3.2cm}", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"]
T.frame(_df_anova, "Analysis of variance of the selected response-surface models with terms.", "tbl-anova", merge=["Output"], align=_al_anova, size="footnotesize", notes=_nt_anova, notes_per_row=True).show()
```

On the log scale the effects on pool host cell protein are fold changes. From the low to the high end of its range, load pH multiplies pool host cell protein by `{python} fx(fold_A)`, so it about halves it, and Equil/Wash-1 conductivity multiplies it by `{python} fx(fold_B)`. The two coefficients, `{python} fx(bA, 3)` and +`{python} fx(bB, 3)` per coded unit, are equal in size within their standard errors (`{python} fx(SEA, 3)` and `{python} fx(SEB, 3)`), so neither parameter is the larger effect. The residual standard deviation on the log scale, `{python} fx(FIT[HCP]["rmse"], 3)`, corresponds to a scatter between runs of about `{python} f"{100 * (mult_sd - 1):.0f}"` % of the level. The block term is `{python} fx(bBlk, 3)` on the log scale (`{python} pe(float(HCPm.pvalues["block"]))`), so the augmentation runs did not differ detectably from the planned runs.

Across its range, load pH raises the XMuLV LRF by `{python} fx(2 * xA)` log10 at the centre of protein load and the MVM LRF by `{python} fx(2 * mA)` log10. Load conductivity lowers them by `{python} fx(-2 * xC)` and `{python} fx(-2 * mC)` log10. For each virus the effects of load pH and load conductivity are equal in size within their standard errors.

The interaction of load pH and protein load makes the effect of protein load on the XMuLV LRF depend on load pH. From the lowest to the highest protein load, the model lowers the XMuLV LRF by `{python} fx(-xD_lo)` log10 at the low end of load pH and raises it by `{python} fx(xD_hi)` log10 at the high end. The interaction is significant (`{python} pe(float(XMm.pvalues["load_ph:load"]))`), and it stays in the selected model, which decides the judgements of this report. Both changes are of the size of the repeatability of the XMuLV assay (`{python} f"{REP_X:g}"` log10), and only one of the two near-equivalent models carries the interaction (@sec-near). It is therefore not established as an effect of protein load.

### The augmentation and the re-evaluation {#sec-reeval}

@tbl-reeval-aex re-evaluates the models with the augmentation runs. On the planned runs the full quadratic model of pool host cell protein failed the limit on overfitting, with R² minus predicted R² of `{python} fx(GAP_FF[HCP])`. On all `{python} n_all` runs with a block term the same model meets the lack of fit test and the limit on overfitting.

```{python}
#| output: asis
T.model_reevaluation("aex").show()
```

Once models are selected, pool host cell protein did not need the augmentation to pass PCMP-001 §7.2. The model selected on the `{python} n_rsm` planned runs alone has the same scale and terms as the model on all runs and meets §7.2. On the planned runs alone it also meets the criterion over the NOR, with the offset at its estimate and at both ends of its interval. A model selected on the same runs it is judged on passes an optimistic check, and the augmentation runs are an independent one. The model selected on the planned runs predicted `{python} int(AUGCHK.loc[HCP, "inside_pi"])` of the `{python} int(AUGCHK.loc[HCP, "n_new"])` augmentation runs inside its 95 % prediction interval for pool host cell protein, and `{python} int(AUGCHK.loc[FRAG, "inside_pi"])` of `{python} int(AUGCHK.loc[FRAG, "n_new"])` for fragments. Step yield is the one output whose model the augmentation changed. On the planned runs alone its selected model, in `{python} tws(FP[YLD]["names"])`, fails the limit on overfitting (`{python} fx(FP[YLD]["gap"])`), and on all runs the selected model contains no term and meets §7.2. Step yield has no criterion.

For pool host cell protein `{python} NE_N[HCP]` models qualify. All contain load pH and Equil/Wash-1 conductivity. Their interaction appears in `{python} HCP_NE_AB` of them, a curvature in load pH in `{python} HCP_NE_A2` and load conductivity in `{python} HCP_NE_C`. None contains the interaction of protein load and Equil/Wash-1 conductivity that marked the invalidated first execution (@sec-dev01). For XMuLV the other model drops protein load and its interaction with load pH. For MVM the two other models add an interaction of load pH and load conductivity or a curvature in load pH.

Under every near-equivalent model each output meets its criterion over the NOR, and the scale-down model stays qualified for pool host cell protein. The lower edge of the NOR-propagated range of load pH lies between `{python} f"{NE_PARLO_MIN[XM]:g}"` and `{python} f"{NE_PARLO_MAX[XM]:g}"` for XMuLV and between `{python} f"{NE_PARLO_MIN[MV]:g}"` and `{python} f"{NE_PARLO_MAX[MV]:g}"` for MVM, below the NOR in every case. The design-space fraction lies between `{python} fx(100 * NE_DSF_MIN, 1)` and `{python} fx(100 * NE_DSF_MAX, 1)` %. For pool host cell protein and fragments the upper 95 % limit of a single run stays below the criterion everywhere on the design-space grid under every model, with the host cell protein offset at the unfavourable end of its interval. Their ranges therefore span the characterized range under every model.

The interaction of load pH and Equil/Wash-1 conductivity on pool host cell protein, which PCP-008 expected, is significant on the raw scale in the screening model (`{python} pe(SE[HCP].loc["AB", "p-value"])`) and in the plan's full quadratic model of the planned response-surface runs (`{python} pe(AB_RAW_P)`). On the log scale it stays significant in the screening data (coefficient `{python} fx(AB_S, 3)`, `{python} pe(AB_S_P)`) and is not significant in the response-surface data (`{python} AB_R_S`, `{python} pe(AB_R_P)`, full quadratic on all runs). The difference between the two log-scale estimates is significant (z = `{python} fx(AB_Z)`, `{python} pe(AB_ZP)`). The data do not identify its cause. The response-surface model, fitted on `{python} n_all` runs, is the predictive model (PCMP-001 §6.2), and no judgement over the NOR changes with or without the interaction.

These lower bounds are set by the assays, not by the step. ## Mechanistic interpretation {#sec-mechanism}

Load pH and Equil/Wash-1 conductivity act on pool host cell protein, and load pH and load conductivity act on the LRFs, in the directions that charge-based binding predicts. A higher load pH moves more of the host cell protein population below its isoelectric point and makes the virus particles more negative, so both bind more strongly. Pool host cell protein falls and both LRFs rise. A higher Equil/Wash-1 conductivity shields the charge of the weakly bound host cell proteins and lets them through.

The log scale of the host cell protein model is the form a purification step gives. Each parameter changes the share of host cell protein that passes, so its effect in ng/mg is larger where the level is higher. That reproduces the dependence of the conductivity effect on load pH that PCP-008 §4.1 expected. In ng/mg, Equil/Wash-1 conductivity raises pool host cell protein more at the low end of load pH than at the high end. On the log scale the response-surface data show no further interaction, and the screening data do (@sec-near).

Two results do not follow the expectations of @sec-platform. Load conductivity acts on both LRFs and not detectably on host cell protein, and Equil/Wash-1 conductivity acts on host cell protein and not detectably on either LRF. The mechanism expected each conductivity to act on both kinds of impurity, and it does not explain this split. One explanation consistent with the data, which this study did not test, is that a virus particle bound at many points of its surface is not released by the salt of the wash. Its capture would then be decided during the load, while weakly bound host cell proteins are displaced during the chase.

Protein load had no detected effect on pool host cell protein, as expected for an impurity mass below the capacity of the ligand. Step yield did not depend on the parameters, as expected for a step in which the antibody does not bind within the load pH range studied.

The invalidated first execution shows how the step responds to a load that is not representative. On a deamidated load, pool host cell protein rose steeply with protein load at high Equil/Wash-1 conductivity, and that interaction is absent from the requalified data (@sec-dev01). PCP-008 §12 expected that a load with more acidic variants carries antibody whose net charge at the load pH is close to neutral, part of which can bind. Bound antibody would occupy ligand that the host cell proteins need, and the salt of the wash would displace the weakly bound proteins first. This study did not test that explanation, and the data are consistent with it.

# Design space {#sec-design-space}

The design space is the region of the four multivariate parameters in which every output with a criterion meets it at once. It is drawn on the single-batch limit for pool host cell protein and fragments and on the mean prediction for viral clearance (PCMP-001 §6.2). On the grid of `{python} DS_N` levels per parameter it covers `{python} fx(100 * DSF, 1)` % of the characterized region. MVM clearance excludes `{python} fx(100 * DS["per_response"][MV], 2)` % of the grid and XMuLV clearance `{python} fx(100 * DS["per_response"][XM], 2)` %, and pool host cell protein and fragments exclude no grid point. With every output on its mean prediction, which serves as a comparison only, the fraction is the same, because the quality attributes exclude nothing on either basis.

The excluded region lies at low load pH and high load conductivity. On the mean prediction at the lowest load pH studied, `{python} f"{P['load_ph'].prange[0]:g}"`, the MVM claim is not met above a load conductivity of `{python} qv("load_cond", BND_MV, 2)`, whatever the protein load and the Equil/Wash-1 conductivity, neither of which enters the MVM model. At the same load pH and the highest protein load studied, `{python} qv("load", P["load"].prange[1])`, the XMuLV claim is not met above `{python} qv("load_cond", BND_XM, 2)`.

The whole NOR lies inside the design space, because every combination of NOR low, set-point and NOR high meets every criterion on its deciding statistic (@tbl-criteria-aex). The design space in turn lies inside the characterized region, the knowledge space of this study. Within the NOR a single run can still fall below a viral claim. At the least favourable combination the lower 95 % limit of a single run is `{python} fx(WC[XM]["pi_low"])` log10 for XMuLV and `{python} fx(WC[MV]["pi_low"])` log10 for MVM. Viral clearance is judged on the mean (@sec-stats), and these single-run limits are given for information.

The design space is a model of the scale-down data. It is not confirmed at scale at its edges, and Stage 2 confirms performance inside the NOR only. Movement within the design space is not a change under ICH Q8(R2), and any planned movement is assessed under the change management of the pharmaceutical quality system [@ichq8; @ichq10].

# Proven acceptable ranges {#sec-par}

## Acceptance basis {#sec-par-basis}

Each output is judged against its intermediate acceptance criterion, derived in PCMP-001 §7.3 from the drug substance criterion and the platform worst case of every downstream step, with no margin (@tbl-iac). No step after anion exchange changes host cell protein or fragments on the platform, so both carry their drug substance criteria, ≤ `{python} HCP_CRIT` and ≤ `{python} FRAG_CRIT`. For the two viruses the step is held to its platform claim, the log reduction it delivered on the platform. The XMuLV claims of low-pH viral inactivation, anion exchange and virus filtration sum to `{python} SUM_X` log10 against a cumulative requirement of `{python} REQ_X` log10. The MVM claims of anion exchange and virus filtration sum to `{python} SUM_M` log10 against `{python} REQ_M` log10 (PCMP-001 §7.4). A shortfall of this step therefore cannot be made up by another step. The derivation uses no data of these studies, and every criterion of this step is in force at its a priori value.

```{python}
#| output: asis
T.iac_derivation(["aex"]).show()
```

## Outputs against their criteria {#sec-par-results}

@tbl-criteria-aex sets each output against its criterion over the NOR, at manufacturing scale where an offset is known. Every output met its criterion. The upper 95 % limit of a single run of pool host cell protein reached at most `{python} fx(NPL_HCP, 1)` ng/mg, which leaves a factor of `{python} fx(MARGIN_HCP, 1)` to the criterion. That of fragments reached at most `{python} fx(NPL_FRAG)` %. The mean LRF at the least favourable combination was `{python} fx(WC_MEAN[XM])` log10 for XMuLV and `{python} fx(WC_MEAN[MV])` log10 for MVM, against claims of `{python} CL_X` and `{python} CL_M` log10. For both viruses that combination has load pH at its NOR low (`{python} f"{WC_SET[XM]['load_ph']:g}"`) and load conductivity at its NOR high (`{python} qv("load_cond", WC_SET[XM]["load_cond"])`), and for XMuLV also protein load at its NOR high (`{python} qv("load", WC_SET[XM]["load"])`). Equil/Wash-1 conductivity enters neither model, and protein load does not enter the MVM model.
